items.gist: The passage distinguishes two kinds of śiva and describes initiation as producing varied results for yogins.
Those with imperfect knowledge become śiva at death, since bodily error ceases and higher knowledge arises.
Those with matured knowledge are ever śiva-may and jīvanmuktas, with no concern at death.
Quotations from Śrīratnamālā and related texts describe a jñānī attaining liberation even in impure places.
The Anantakārikā is cited to deny karmic bondage and to state that death does not cause liberation.
For the jīvanmukta, connection with one's own body is no more individuating than connection with another body.
The text affirms kevalatva and cites Triśira on the jñānī pervading all things like space in a pot.
The jñānī, free from aversion and obstruction, is Śiva-maya and independent while pervading all things.
A Gītā verse is cited on remembering the Lord at death, followed by discussion of gradual dissolution of qualities.
The final moment of life is described as the last breath, after which the body becomes inert.
At death one assumes the form most remembered, whether mixed with pleasure and pain or blissful.
Consciousness rests upon a prior substrate, and the body is distinguished by being pervaded by consciousness.
The body's special relation to consciousness is explained through its constant and repeated embodiment.
Kallaṭa's reasoning addresses why bodily continuity and memory determine the form assumed at death.
Memory of a prior body is not direct knowledge of another body, but latent impressions may arise at death.
A purāṇic example of a sage becoming a deer illustrates how latent impressions shape experience without creating new births.
Bhāvanā is the gradual clarification of what is to be, not the experience of what is already clear.
Even in dullness, prior impressions become clear at death through memory and saṃskāra.
The text discusses whether such impressions produce a similar body and companions in another world.
The dream analogy is challenged, since no other cognizer is directly perceived.
Existence of other cognizers and objects is established in consciousness, not in the objects themselves.
